Q011405:
## Looking at one continuous feature
Before choosing a transformation or an algorithm, a practitioner looks at the distribution of each feature: is it symmetric, skewed, multimodal, or does it contain extreme values? The distribution of a single continuous variable is shown by a histogram, which splits the value range into bins and shows how many rows fall in each. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis practice.
## In Databricks
Notebook and SQL editor visualizations include a histogram type. The Databricks documentation describes it as plotting how frequently a value occurs, showing whether values cluster around a few ranges or are spread out, as a bar chart in which you control the number of bins. Histogram charts also support backend aggregation, so queries over more than 64,000 rows are not truncated.
- A long right tail and several peaks are both visible at a glance; changing the bin count shows more or less detail.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Histogram (correct):** it shows how often values fall into each range, so skew (a long tail on one side) and clusters (several peaks) are visible directly, and the bin count can be tuned.
- ✗ **B. Counter display:** a counter shows one aggregate number such as the mean. A single average cannot reveal skew or clusters, which is exactly what the question asks about.
- ✗ **C. Word cloud:** a word cloud sizes words by frequency and is meant for text. Numbers as words give no sense of value ranges or ordering.
- ✗ **D. Pie chart:** a pie chart shows the proportion of a whole across a few categories; ten arbitrary slices hide the shape of a continuous distribution and are hard to compare by eye.

## Key idea
To see the shape of one continuous feature, use a histogram (bins show skew and clusters), not a pie, counter or word cloud.
Q011406:
## Continuous values grouped by a category
When one feature is numeric and the other categorical, the useful question is how the numeric distribution differs between groups. A box plot summarizes each group with its median, quartiles (the interquartile range) and whiskers or outlying points, so groups can be compared side by side. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis technique.
## In Databricks
The box chart visualization in notebooks and the SQL editor shows the distribution summary of numerical data, optionally grouped by a category. The documentation says it lets you compare value ranges across categories and see the location, spread and skewness of groups through their quartiles. The docs also note that box charts aggregate only up to 64,000 rows; larger datasets are truncated, so sample or aggregate first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pie chart:** a pie shows proportions of a whole across a few categories; one slice per fare value is unreadable and carries no quartile information.
- ✗ **B. Line chart by row number:** row order is arbitrary here, so the line shows no per-category summary and mixes all payment types together.
- ✗ **C. Scatter chart:** a scatter chart shows the relationship between two numeric variables. Putting a categorical column on both axes produces only a grid of identical points and says nothing about the spread of fares.
- ✓ **D. Box chart (correct):** it draws one box per category with median, interquartile range and outlying values, which is the per-group spread comparison the analyst asked for.

## Key idea
Numeric spread per category is a box chart (median, quartiles, outliers per group); histograms show one distribution, scatter charts show two numeric variables.
Q011407:
## Frequencies of a categorical feature
A categorical feature has no meaningful numeric distribution, so the usual check is a count per category. A bar chart with one bar per category shows class balance (for example, 90% / 8% / 2%), which matters because imbalanced labels change how a model is trained and evaluated. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis practice.
## In Databricks
For bar, line, area, pie and heatmap charts the visualization editor can aggregate the Y-axis column itself (for example a count), so you do not rewrite the query to add an aggregation column. The documentation points out that this aggregation applies to the entire dataset, not just the first 64,000 rows shown in a table. Bar charts also support backend aggregation, so queries returning more than 64K rows are not truncated.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Scatter chart:** a scatter chart plots two numeric variables. Fifty million points for a three-valued category would overlap into three lines and show no counts.
- ✗ **B. Box chart:** a box chart summarizes a numeric value per category; the label has no numeric value to summarize and the chart would not display class counts.
- ✓ **C. Bar chart with visualization aggregation (correct):** counting rows per category in the chart settings shows the class proportions over the full dataset without editing the underlying query.
- ✗ **D. Histogram with many narrow bins:** a histogram bins a numeric range. A categorical label has no range, so most bins would be empty.

## Key idea
Class balance of a categorical feature is a bar chart of counts per category; let the visualization aggregate over the whole dataset.
Q011408:
## Display rows versus the full dataset
A notebook result table shows a limited number of rows. If a visualization is built on those displayed rows with no aggregation, the chart reflects only that subset, and a statistic computed from it can differ from the same statistic over all rows. This is why a plotted average can disagree with a Spark aggregation.
## The Databricks fix
The documentation says that for bar, line, area, pie and heatmap charts you can turn on aggregation in the visualization itself, and that the aggregation applies to the entire dataset rather than the first 64,000 rows displayed in a table. Alternatively aggregate in the query first and plot the small result.
- A summary computed in Spark (`groupBy`) always uses all rows; the chart on a truncated table does not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Region name length:** `avg` groups by the whole value of `region`, whatever its length; this is not how grouping works.
- ✓ **B. First 64,000 rows (correct):** the chart used only the displayed subset, so its averages are estimates from that subset. Turn on the chart's aggregation or aggregate in the query to use all 12 million rows.
- ✗ **C. Rounding:** bar charts do not round values to integers; the small differences are not whole-number rounding.
- ✗ **D. Stale cache:** a cleared cache would cause a recompute, not different averages, and the chart is built from the cell's own result, not from a previous cluster.

## Key idea
A chart on a displayed table covers only the first 64,000 rows; enable the visualization aggregation (whole dataset) or aggregate in the query.
Q011409:
## What a distribution view must show
The distribution of a continuous feature is its spread: center, range, skew and outliers. Two standard exploratory charts do this for one variable: the histogram (frequency per bin) and the box plot (median, quartiles, outlying values). This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis definition.
## Databricks chart types
Notebook and SQL editor visualizations include histogram and box charts. Pie charts show proportions of categories, counter displays show a single number, and word clouds show text frequency.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Word cloud:** sizes words by frequency; it is a text visual, not a numeric distribution.
- ✗ **B. Pie chart:** shows shares of categories, not a continuous spread.
- ✓ **C. Histogram (correct):** bins of the value range show shape, skew and clusters of one feature.
- ✗ **D. Counter display:** gives one headline number such as an average and no information about shape or spread.
- ✓ **E. Box chart (correct):** shows median, interquartile range and outlying points of one numeric feature, and can be grouped by a category if needed.

## Key idea
Histogram and box chart are the single-variable distribution views for a continuous feature.
Q011410:
## Two continuous features
For two numeric features the standard question is how strongly one changes with the other. The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship on a scale from -1 to 1; Spearman correlation does the same for rank (monotonic) relationships. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## In Spark ML
`pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation` computes a correlation matrix over a vector column and supports the methods Pearson (default) and Spearman. The chi-squared test, by contrast, requires categorical features and labels.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Comparing modes:** modes describe the most frequent value of each column separately and say nothing about how the two columns vary together.
- ✗ **B. Chi-squared test:** Spark's `ChiSquareTest` converts feature/label pairs into a contingency matrix and requires categorical values, so raw continuous columns do not fit.
- ✗ **C. Distinct counts:** cardinality describes each column separately and is unrelated to joint movement.
- ✓ **D. Pearson correlation (correct):** it gives a single number between -1 and 1 describing the linear association of the two continuous columns, and Spark ML computes it with `Correlation.corr`.

## Key idea
Two continuous features are compared with correlation (Pearson for linear, Spearman for monotonic); chi-squared needs categorical data.
Q011411:
## Association between categorical variables
For two categorical variables the standard test is Pearson's chi-squared test of independence. It builds a contingency table of observed counts, compares it with the counts expected if the variables were independent, and returns a statistic and p-value. This is a generally accepted statistical definition.
## In Spark ML
The Spark documentation states that `spark.ml` supports Pearson's chi-squared tests for independence. `ChiSquareTest` runs the test for every feature against the label; the (feature, label) pairs are converted into a contingency matrix, and all label and feature values must be categorical.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. OneHotEncoder:** it transforms categories into vectors for modeling. It is a preprocessing step and gives no p-value.
- ✓ **B. ChiSquareTest (correct):** it tests independence of each categorical feature against a categorical label and returns p-values, matching the question.
- ✗ **C. Imputer with mode:** Imputer fills missing values; it does not test any relationship (and Spark documents that it does not support categorical features).
- ✗ **D. Spearman correlation:** it ranks numeric values; arbitrary category indices have no meaningful order, so a rank correlation of them is not an independence test.

## Key idea
Categorical-vs-categorical independence is a chi-squared test (`ChiSquareTest` in Spark ML), which needs categorical inputs.
Q011412:
## Choosing the comparison by feature types
The right statistic depends on the types of the two features.
- Continuous vs continuous: correlation (Pearson or Spearman).
- Categorical vs categorical: chi-squared test of independence.
- Continuous vs a two-level categorical: compare the group means with a two-sample t-test (or a rank-based test when the data are not normal); with more than two groups, an ANOVA. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## On Databricks
Spark ML ships correlation and chi-squared tests in `pyspark.ml.stat`; group-mean tests such as the t-test are usually done on a sample with `scipy.stats` (single node) or by comparing group aggregates and a box chart.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Two-sample t-test (correct):** it tests whether the means of a continuous variable differ between two groups, which is exactly a continuous feature split by a two-level categorical feature.
- ✗ **B. Correlation of a column with itself:** this is trivially 1 and tells nothing about group differences.
- ✗ **C. Bar chart of distinct values:** that is a frequency view of one column and does not compare group means.
- ✗ **D. Chi-squared:** Spark's version needs categorical values; a continuous variable would have to be binned first, losing information.

## Key idea
Match the test to the types: numeric-numeric is correlation, category-category is chi-squared, numeric by two groups is a t-test.
Q011413:
## What a correlation coefficient measures
Pearson's coefficient measures the strength of a linear relationship. A symmetric curve such as a U or parabola has positive slope on one side and negative on the other, so the linear effects cancel and the coefficient is near zero even though `y` is a deterministic function of `x`. A coefficient near zero therefore means "no linear association", not "no association". This is a generally accepted statistical fact.
- Always plot the two features (scatter chart) before trusting a single number.
- Spearman measures monotonic association and would also miss a U shape; a transformation (such as squaring) or a nonlinear model can capture it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Chart error:** the chart is right; opposing slopes cancel and produce a near-zero coefficient.
- ✗ **B. Zero means independent:** zero correlation does not imply independence; here `y` depends on `x` completely.
- ✗ **C. Replace with the mean:** Pearson is valid for linear relationships; the mean is a one-column summary and says nothing about two variables together.
- ✓ **D. Strong but nonlinear (correct):** the two sides of the U cancel in a linear measure, so the near-zero Pearson value is consistent with a clear dependence, which the scatter chart reveals.

## Key idea
Correlation near zero means no linear relationship only; check a scatter chart for nonlinear patterns.
Q011414:
## Collinear features
When two predictors are almost perfectly correlated (multicollinearity), they carry nearly the same information. A linear model cannot separate their effects, so coefficients become unstable and hard to interpret even when predictions stay fine. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
- Remove one of the pair, keeping the one that is easier to collect or explain.
- Combine them into one feature (a component from PCA, or a domain ratio or difference).
Correlation is computed in Spark ML with `Correlation.corr` (Pearson default).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Drop one (correct):** the remaining feature keeps almost all the information and the coefficient instability disappears.
- ✗ **B. Mode imputation:** nothing in the question concerns missing values, and the mode of a continuous column is not a fix for collinearity.
- ✗ **C. Spearman:** it is a different way to measure association; computing it does not change the data or remove the dependency.
- ✗ **D. One-hot encoding:** that is for categorical features; numeric columns are not made independent by it.
- ✓ **E. Combine into one (correct):** a principal component or ratio keeps the shared signal in one column and removes the redundancy.

## Key idea
Highly correlated predictors are redundant: drop one or merge them (PCA, ratio) rather than keeping both in a linear model.
Q011415:
## Choosing mean, median or mode
- The **mean** uses every value, so a few extreme values pull it away from a typical row.
- The **median** is the middle value and barely moves when outliers are added, so it is the usual choice for skewed numeric data.
- The **mode** is the most frequent value; it is the natural fill for categorical data.
These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## In Spark ML
`Imputer` fills missing values with the mean (default), median or mode of the column. The median is computed with `approxQuantile` using a relative error of 0.001.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean:** extreme values drag the mean upward, so filled rows would get an unrealistically high income.
- ✓ **B. Median (correct):** it is the middle value, so a handful of very large incomes do not shift it, and it represents a typical household in a skewed column.
- ✗ **C. Mode:** for a continuous income column the most frequent exact value is usually arbitrary (many values appear once) and is not a stable center.
- ✗ **D. Maximum:** it is the most extreme value and would make every filled row an outlier.

## Key idea
Skewed numeric column: impute the median; mean suits symmetric data and mode suits categorical data.
Q011416:
## Imputing categorical data
Mean and median need numbers with a meaningful order and distance. A nominal category such as "card" has neither, so the mean and median of labels are not defined. The mode, the most frequent value, is defined for any data type, so it is the standard simple fill for categorical features. Another option is a separate "missing" category. These are generally accepted data-preparation practices.
## In Spark ML
Spark's `Imputer` supports numeric columns only and documents that it does not support categorical features. For a string column, compute the mode with a `groupBy().count()` and fill with `fillna`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean of counts:** a count is not a label; rounding it cannot produce a valid category.
- ✗ **B. Median of string lengths:** this returns a number, not a payment method, and has no connection to the missing category.
- ✓ **C. Mode (correct):** the most frequent category is a valid label for any categorical column and keeps the column's value set unchanged.
- ✗ **D. Mean of labels:** strings have no meaningful average; alphabetical position would invent an order that does not exist.

## Key idea
Impute categorical features with the mode (or an explicit "missing" category); mean and median are for numeric data.
Q011417:
## Symmetric versus skewed data
For symmetric data the mean, median and mode coincide, so the choice matters little and the mean is cheap and exact. Skew separates them. These are generally accepted statistical facts.
Mean imputation has known side effects: every filled row gets the same value, so the column's variance shrinks and its correlations with other features are weakened. With few missing values these effects are small.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Adds new information:** a constant fill carries no row-specific information; it only avoids dropping the row.
- ✗ **B. Increases variance:** filling with a constant reduces variance because the filled rows sit exactly at the center.
- ✗ **C. Always more robust:** it is the reverse, the median is the robust statistic.
- ✓ **D. Mean and median nearly coincide (correct):** filling with the mean leaves the column's center where it was and is a sensible default when the data are symmetric and have no outliers.

## Key idea
Mean imputation is fine for symmetric data with few gaps, but it shrinks variance; use the median for skewed data.
Q011418:
## What a constant fill does
Replacing every missing value with the mean adds rows exactly at the center. Hence the mean is unchanged, the variance falls (more rows with zero deviation), and the covariance with other features falls too, so correlations are weakened. This is a generally accepted statistical fact, which is why large amounts of missingness call for model-based imputation or an indicator column.
## Spark detail
`Imputer(strategy="mean")` is the default and works on numeric columns only.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mean unchanged (correct):** adding values equal to the mean does not move the mean of the column.
- ✗ **B. Row-specific values:** mean imputation uses one value for the whole column; neighbor-based fills are a different method.
- ✗ **C. Categorical columns:** a mean of strings is undefined, and Spark's Imputer documents that it does not support categorical features.
- ✗ **D. Strengthens correlations:** a constant carries no co-movement with other features, so correlations weaken.
- ✓ **E. Variance shrinks (correct):** the new rows have zero deviation from the mean, so the spread of the column falls.

## Key idea
Mean imputation keeps the mean, lowers variance and weakens correlations; use it sparingly.
Q011419:
## Leakage in preprocessing
Any statistic learned from data (a median, a mean, a mode) is a parameter of the model pipeline. If it is computed on all rows before the split, the training set contains information about the test rows, and the evaluation no longer simulates unseen data. The generally accepted practice is to split first, compute the fill values on the training set only, and apply those same values to the test set and to new data at serving time.
## In Spark ML
`Imputer` is an estimator: `fit` on the training DataFrame learns the surrogate values, and the resulting model's `transform` applies them to any other DataFrame.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Type change:** splitting rows only separates the rows into two DataFrames and does not change any column type, so it cannot explain a leak or an optimistic score.
- ✓ **B. Leakage (correct):** the median came from all rows including test rows, so the test set influenced the preprocessing; fitting only on training data removes the leak.
- ✗ **C. Cannot split after imputation:** Spark can split any DataFrame at any time with `randomSplit`.
- ✗ **D. Always inflates:** there is no inflation when the statistic is fitted on the training data only.

## Key idea
Fit imputation statistics on the training data only and reuse them on test and serving data.
Q011420:
## How Imputer works
`Imputer` is an estimator. `fit` computes one surrogate value per input column from the non-missing values, using the configured strategy (`mean` default, `median` or `mode`), and returns an `ImputerModel`. `transform` writes the surrogate into the output column wherever the input equals the missing value. The default missing value is `NaN`, and the documentation says all `null` values in the input columns are treated as missing too.
- Median is calculated with `approxQuantile` and a relative error of 0.001.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zero:** no zero is used; the surrogate is computed from the data unless `setMissingValue` changes what counts as missing.
- ✗ **B. Null stays null:** the documentation states that all nulls in the input columns are treated as missing and are imputed.
- ✓ **C. Median for both (correct):** the strategy is median, and null and NaN are both treated as missing, so both are replaced by the median of the remaining values.
- ✗ **D. Mean:** the strategy was explicitly set to median; the mean is only the default when no strategy is given.

## Key idea
Imputer replaces NaN and null with the mean, median or mode of the non-missing numeric values, using the strategy you set.
Q011421:
## Sentinel values
Some systems write a placeholder such as `-999` instead of null. By default Imputer treats only `NaN` and `null` as missing, so the placeholder would be treated as a real value and would distort the median. The `missingValue` parameter changes which value is regarded as missing (the docs show `setMissingValue(0)` imputing every 0). The surrogate is calculated from the other values, excluding the missing ones.
- Always check for sentinel values in the data summary (a minimum of -999 is the hint).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean with missingValue 0:** this would impute genuine zero distances and use the wrong strategy.
- ✗ **B. relativeError:** this parameter controls the accuracy of the approximate median, not which value counts as missing, so the -999 sentinels stay in the data.
- ✗ **C. Mode with defaults:** only NaN/null count as missing, so the sentinels stay and also affect the mode.
- ✓ **D. Median with `missingValue=-999.0` (correct):** it marks the sentinel as missing, computes the median of the genuine distances, and writes it into the new column.

## Key idea
Use `missingValue` to tell Imputer which sentinel (such as -999) means "missing"; NaN and null are always treated as missing.
Q011422:
## Imputer and strings
Spark's `Imputer` input columns should be numeric. The documentation says it does not support categorical features and may create incorrect values for them, even with `strategy="mode"`.
For a string column do it by hand: count each value, take the most frequent non-null one (for example `df.groupBy("city").count().orderBy("count", ascending=False)`), and fill with `df.fillna({"city": top_city})`. If the column is going to be one-hot encoded afterwards, `StringIndexer` with `handleInvalid="keep"` is another way to give missing values their own index.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. missingValue empty string:** that only changes which numeric value counts as missing; it does not make the input type accepted.
- ✗ **B. Mean strategy:** mean is not defined for strings, and Imputer does not support categorical features for any strategy.
- ✓ **C. groupBy plus fillna (correct):** this finds the real mode of the strings and writes it into the missing rows, which Imputer cannot do for text.
- ✗ **D. Cast to float:** strings such as city names become null on a cast, losing all information and imputing nothing meaningful.

## Key idea
Imputer is numeric-only; impute a categorical string column with its mode using a groupBy count and `fillna`.
Q011423:
## Estimator and model
`Imputer` is an estimator: calling `fit` on the training data learns a surrogate value per column and returns an `ImputerModel` (a transformer). The model stores those learned values and later `transform` calls only apply them. This keeps preprocessing consistent between training and serving, and it avoids leakage because the scoring data never influences the fill value.
- If the scoring batch had its own median computed, the same row could be filled differently on different days and in a different batch composition than in training.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recompute at scoring:** a transformer does not learn; only `fit` computes statistics.
- ✓ **B. Learned training median (correct):** the `ImputerModel` keeps the surrogate values from `fit`, so new batches are filled with the same values used in training.
- ✗ **C. Mean of the batch:** the strategy was median and values come from training, not from the batch.
- ✗ **D. Works only in training:** a fitted model's `transform` is what runs at scoring time.

## Key idea
Fit once on training data; the ImputerModel reuses the stored values for every later batch.
Q011424:
## Imputer facts
From the Spark documentation: Imputer is an estimator that completes missing values using the mean, median or mode of the columns where values are missing. Input columns must be numeric; categorical features are not supported. The default `strategy` is `mean`. All nulls are treated as missing, and `missingValue` (default NaN) can be changed. The statistic is computed after filtering out missing values.
- Because it is an estimator, you call `fit` first and use the resulting `ImputerModel` to `transform`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mean, median and mode on numeric columns (correct):** this matches the documented behavior, with mean the default strategy.
- ✗ **B. Mean only on any type:** median and mode are supported, and categorical columns are not.
- ✗ **C. Transformer without fit:** Imputer is an estimator whose `fit` computes the surrogate values.
- ✗ **D. Median default on strings:** the default is mean, and string columns are not supported.

## Key idea
Imputer: numeric columns, strategy mean (default), median or mode; fit then transform.
Q011425:
## Why nominal categories are not integers
A linear model multiplies a feature by one weight. If `colour` is a single integer, the model assumes green is "between" red and blue, and that the effect of moving from 0 to 2 is twice that from 0 to 1. For a nominal category that is false.
One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column (or a vector with a single 1), so each category can have its own weight. The Spark documentation notes that this encoding lets algorithms that expect continuous features, such as logistic regression, use categorical features. The ordering problem is a generally accepted modeling fact.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Implied order and spacing (correct):** with integer codes the model sees ordered, equally spaced numbers; one-hot columns let each colour carry its own coefficient.
- ✗ **B. Cannot read numerics:** logistic regression works on numeric inputs; the issue is the meaning of the numbers.
- ✗ **C. Memory:** one-hot vectors use more space, not less, and the reason for encoding is correctness.
- ✗ **D. Normal distribution:** indicator columns are binary, so they are not normally distributed.

## Key idea
Nominal categories should be one-hot encoded for linear models so no false order or spacing is implied.
Q011426:
## From strings to a feature vector
`OneHotEncoder` expects category indices as input, not strings. The Spark documentation says that for string data it is common to encode categories with `StringIndexer` first. Its output vector column is then commonly merged with the numeric columns into one vector with `VectorAssembler`.
- `StringIndexer` maps `country` to an index (most frequent first by default).
- `OneHotEncoder` turns the index into a binary vector.
- `VectorAssembler` combines the encoded vector with `age` and `income` into a `features` column.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Encoder before indexer:** the encoder would receive raw strings, which it does not accept.
- ✗ **B. Assembler first:** the assembler would receive a string column and have nothing numeric to combine for `country`.
- ✗ **C. Assembler before encoder:** the indices would be merged as plain numbers into the vector before they are one-hot encoded, so the category would be treated as an ordered value.
- ✓ **D. Index, encode, assemble (correct):** each stage consumes the previous output, ending with one feature vector for the estimator.

## Key idea
StringIndexer, then OneHotEncoder, then VectorAssembler.
Q011427:
## The dropLast default
The Spark documentation explains that the last category is not included by default (`dropLast=True`) because including it would make the entries of each vector sum to one, which are linearly dependent. With 5 categories the output length is therefore 4: index 2 maps to `[0, 0, 1, 0]`, and index 4 (the last category) maps to `[0, 0, 0, 0]`.
- Set `dropLast=False` to keep a full length-5 vector.
- Tree-based and linear models can both use the reduced form; the missing category is represented by "all zeros".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single 4.0:** that would be the original index, not a one-hot vector.
- ✓ **B. All zeros of length 4 (correct):** dropLast is true by default, so the final category is the baseline with no indicator.
- ✗ **C. All ones:** a one-hot vector has at most one entry equal to one.
- ✗ **D. Length 5:** that is the result of `dropLast=False`, which was not set.

## Key idea
Default `dropLast=True` gives N-1 columns; the last category is all zeros.
Q011428:
## Unseen categories
`StringIndexer` is fitted on training data and knows only the labels it saw. Its `handleInvalid` parameter defaults to `error`, so unseen labels throw an exception at transform time. Other options are `skip` (drop the row) and `keep` (put unseen labels at an extra index equal to the number of labels).
`OneHotEncoder` also has `handleInvalid` with `error` (default) and `keep`; with `keep` an extra category is added as the last one, so with `dropLast=True` invalid values become an all-zero vector.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lower case:** this affects spelling only, and a truly new country would still be unseen.
- ✗ **B. Drop the encoder:** the model was trained with encoded features and would receive a different input.
- ✓ **C. handleInvalid="keep" (correct):** unseen countries are mapped to an extra index and encoded instead of raising an error, so the batch is still scored.
- ✗ **D. dropLast:** it changes how many columns the vector has and does not affect how unknown labels are handled.

## Key idea
Use handleInvalid="keep" so unseen categories get an extra index instead of failing; "skip" would drop the rows.
Q011429:
## What OneHotEncoder does
From the Spark documentation: `OneHotEncoder` maps a categorical feature represented as a label index to a binary vector with at most a single one-value, allowing algorithms that expect continuous features, such as logistic regression, to use categorical features. It can transform multiple columns and returns one output vector column for each input column; the outputs are usually merged with `VectorAssembler`. For strings, index them with `StringIndexer` first. `handleInvalid` is `error` or `keep`, and `dropLast` defaults to `True`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Multiple columns (correct):** the encoder accepts `inputCols` and `outputCols` lists and returns a vector column for each input.
- ✗ **B. Mean imputation:** that is `Imputer`; the encoder does not fill missing values.
- ✗ **C. Raw strings:** the encoder takes category indices, so strings must go through `StringIndexer` first.
- ✗ **D. Keeps all categories:** `dropLast=True` by default, so the last category is omitted.

## Key idea
OneHotEncoder turns indexed categories into binary vectors, handles many columns at once, drops the last category by default and needs StringIndexer for strings.
